clue.text: Hasn't realistic expectations, to begin with, constructing these?

indicators.note: constructing means building, so the letters gathered before it are the materials to be put together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, without its apostrophe
taken as written

indicators.note: to begin with points at the opening letter of the word just before it, expectations

explanation.surface: A dreamer with no sensible hopes at the outset is busy building something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constructing' rearranges HASNT REALISTIC plus E, the letter 'to begin with' takes from expectations. The whole clue describes the answer too: a dreamer with no realistic expectations builds 'these'.
explanation.definitionFit: By idiom, hopes and plans with no chance of coming true are fantasies a dreamer is said to build, which is what the whole clue describes.

clue.text: During part of weekend, group introduces live dance music

indicators.note: during means in the course of, so the pieces after the comma sit inside the word for part of the weekend

parts.note: Sat is the usual short form of Saturday, one of the two days of the weekend

indicators.note: introduces means leads in, so the group word comes straight before the word for live

parts.note: a wing is a group within a larger body, such as a party's left wing or an air force unit
to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: A band brings in dance music, played live, for part of the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'During' wraps the weekend day round both other pieces, which 'introduces' keeps in clue order. 'live' suggests music played on stage, but here it is a verb; swingbeat, or new jack swing, is a late-1980s blend of R&B and hip-hop.
explanation.definitionFit: A type of it: a late-1980s blend of R&B and hip-hop rhythms, also known as new jack swing, made for clubs.

clue.text: Starts to grow unusual assorted vegetables and fruit

indicators.note: starts to asks for the opening letter of each of the five words that follow it

explanation.surface: A gardener begins raising an odd mixture of vegetables and fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' takes the opening letters of the next five words. The trap is 'and': it looks like a mere joining word before the definition, but it supplies the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An example of the category: a tropical produce item with pink or white flesh, often juiced or made into jelly.

clue.text: Cruel invader landed, confronting troops in retreat

indicators.note: an army in retreat goes back the way it came, so the two pieces before it are read backwards as one run
confronting means coming face to face with, so the word for landed is set directly against the troops

parts.note: alit is the past tense of alight, to come down and settle, as a bird or a passenger does
TA stands for the Territorial Army, the old name of Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A brutal conqueror comes ashore and faces soldiers who are falling back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confronting' sets ALIT against TA, and 'in retreat' turns the whole run, ALITTA, backwards. TA is the Territorial Army, the old name of Britain's volunteer reserve force.
explanation.definitionFit: An example by reputation: the fifth-century king of the Huns, nicknamed the Scourge of God, who ravaged much of the Roman Empire.

clue.text: Loaded a firearm at the front? Easy

indicators.note: at the front points to the opening letter of the word just before it, firearm

parts.note: fluent speech or movement is easy and flowing, done without effort

explanation.surface: A soldier in the front line put bullets in a gun and found it simple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the front' takes only the first letter of firearm. 'Loaded' suggests a gun with bullets in it, but here it is slang for rich.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: someone described this way has plenty of money, and the answer is the formal adjective for wealthy.

clue.text: News magazine is in French — fancy going first?

indicators.note: going first says the word for fancy is placed ahead of the French word, though the clue names it second

parts.note: to dig something is dated slang for liking it, which in British English is to fancy it
est is the French word for is, as in c'est la vie

explanation.surface: A current-affairs weekly is printed in French; would you like to read it before anyone else?
explanation.walkthrough: 'going first' means the word for fancy leads, though the clue mentions it last. The dash and question mark are only surface dressing, and 'in French' asks for a translation, not a magazine printed in that language.
explanation.definitionFit: A publishing synonym: a periodical that condenses reports and articles from other sources into short summaries.

clue.text: Newspaper shows British monarch at helm of ship

indicators.note: whoever is at the helm is in charge and leading the way, so the pieces before these words go ahead of the ship

parts.note: B is a standard abbreviation for British, as in BBC
ER, for Elizabeth Regina, was the cipher of Queen Elizabeth II, Britain's monarch when this puzzle appeared
a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: A paper prints a picture of the British sovereign steering a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at helm of' places British and the monarch in the lead. The answer is a page size between tabloid and broadsheet, used by Britain's Guardian from 2005 to 2018, and so a name for a paper printed that way.
explanation.definitionFit: An example by format: a paper printed on these mid-sized pages, between tabloid and broadsheet, takes the format's name.

clue.text: Very unpleasant lad Freud treated

indicators.note: treated means processed or worked on, as a patient or a material is, so the two words before it are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sigmund Freud took on a thoroughly nasty boy as a patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' is the signal to rearrange LAD FREUD, not a mention of therapy. The definition is only 'Very unpleasant': the lad belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that inspires dread is extremely bad or disagreeable.

clue.text: Switching starters, keep on at mother to supply bottle of wine

indicators.note: starters are opening letters, and switching them means the two words that follow trade their first letters with each other

parts.note: to nag someone is to keep on at them, pestering without let-up
mum is the everyday British word for mother

explanation.surface: After swapping first courses, a diner pesters Mum to bring a bottle of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switching starters' makes NAG and MUM trade first letters. The surface means first courses at dinner, but the starters are the opening letters of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A size of it: a large one holding 1.5 litres, twice the standard measure, used especially for champagne.

clue.text: Staircase fitted with a new window

indicators.note: fitted with means equipped with, so the staircase word has what follows installed inside it

parts.note: a flight is a continuous run of stairs between two floors
N is the standard abbreviation for new, as in NT for New Testament

explanation.surface: Builders have put a replacement window in beside the stairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fitted with' installs A and N inside FLIGHT. A fanlight is the small window above a door, often a half-circle with bars spread like the ribs of a fan.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind of it: the small pane above a door, often semicircular with glazing bars that radiate like ribs.

clue.text: Hit by popular musician

indicators.note: by means next to, so the word for hit stands right beside the word for popular

parts.note: a chop is a sharp downward blow, as in karate, and to chop is to strike that way
something that is in is fashionable, popular at the moment

explanation.surface: A chart success recorded by a well-loved performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' sets CHOP beside IN. The surface suggests a chart success from a pop star, but 'Hit' is a blow and the musician is a Polish composer of the Romantic era.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: Frederic of that name was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the Romantic era.

clue.text: Small place to keep fish — smelt?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a tank is a glass container of water in which pet fish are kept

explanation.surface: A little aquarium that might hold a smelt, a small silvery fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces sit side by side with no indicator. 'smelt' suggests the small silvery fish of that name, but it is the past tense of smell, in the sense of giving off a bad odour.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms in the past tense: both verbs mean gave off an unpleasant odour, the definition being a British spelling of smelled.

clue.text: Charge towards creature's hideout, circulating like a hawk?

parts.note: a rap is a criminal charge, as in a murder rap or beating the rap
to is the preposition meaning towards, as in walk to the door

indicators.note: circulating means going round, which the setter stretches to mean turned round, so the hideout word is read backwards

parts.note: a lair is the den where a wild animal hides and rests

explanation.surface: Someone rushes at an animal's den, wheeling around it the way a hawk does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circulating' is asked to mean turned round, so the hideout is written backwards; it has nothing to do with a bird wheeling overhead. The question mark shows a hawk is only one example of the predatory birds meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for predatory: the adjective describes birds of prey and their seizing habits, of which the bird named is a typical example.

clue.text: Warmer after sport, drinks liquid to conserve energy

indicators.note: after sport says the pieces that follow in the clue come behind the word for the sport

parts.note: polo is a team sport played on horseback with mallets and a ball
to neck a drink is British slang for gulping it down, so someone who drinks necks

indicators.note: to conserve is to keep safe, so the liquid word keeps the energy letter inside it

parts.note: water is the most familiar liquid
E is the physics symbol for energy, as in E = mc squared

explanation.surface: Feeling hotter once the game is over, a player sips fluids to keep their strength up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' fixes the order and 'to conserve' tucks energy inside the liquid. 'Warmer' looks like a comparison but is a noun, a thing that warms; to neck a drink is British slang for gulping it down.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a knitted garment with a high, close-fitting rolled collar keeps the wearer cosy, so it is a thing that warms.

clue.text: Kid gobbles up peaches and apple

indicators.note: gobbles means swallows greedily, so the word for kid takes the next piece inside it

parts.note: to cod someone is British and Irish slang for hoaxing or teasing them, which is to kid them

indicators.note: in a down entry up means towards the top, so the word for peaches is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: to peach on someone is old slang for informing on them, just as someone rats on an accomplice

explanation.surface: A child wolfs down some peaches and an apple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gobbles up' reads as one phrase but splits: 'gobbles' is the swallowing and 'up' turns the word for peaches upside down. That word is a verb: to peach on someone is old slang for informing on them, as a rat does.
explanation.definitionFit: A variety of it: a large, ribbed English cooking fruit, sold in the past by street traders called costermongers.

clue.text: He wrote flier

definitions.meaning: a male author named only by what he did: this Anglo-Irish satirist wrote Gulliver's Travels in 1726
a flier is anything that flies: here a fast, sickle-winged bird that feeds and even sleeps on the wing

explanation.surface: A man produced the text of a leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'flier' looks like a leaflet the man wrote, but the clue is two definitions side by side: a writer, then something that flies.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the satirist who wrote Gulliver's Travels is also the name of a fast, sickle-winged bird.

clue.text: Allowed crop to be lifted and taken outside

indicators.note: outside says the word for taken goes round the outer edge of the lifted crop

parts.note: someone taken to a place was led there

indicators.note: in a down entry lifted means raised towards the top, so the crop word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: silage is a green crop such as grass, cut and stored in a silo as winter feed for cattle

explanation.surface: The farmer got permission for the harvest to be gathered and carried out of the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be lifted' turns the crop upside down, and 'outside' wraps the word for taken round it. To lift a crop is farmers' talk for harvesting it; the one wanted is green feed stored for winter.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym in the legal sense: something made lawful has been officially permitted.

clue.text: Bird initially startled by sound of cat

indicators.note: by means next to, so the letter from startled stands beside the cat's sound
initially points to the opening letter of the word right after it, startled

parts.note: mew is the thin, high cry a cat makes

explanation.surface: A bird is at first frightened when it hears a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes the first letter of startled and 'by' sets it beside MEW. 'sound of cat' is literal: the noise the animal makes.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a small black-and-white diving duck of northern Europe and Asia, related to the mergansers.

clue.text: Teller no doubt employed in bank

indicators.note: employed in means put to work within, so the word for doubt goes inside the word for bank

parts.note: a bank is a row or tier of things, such as a bank of seats or switches
an if is a doubt or uncertainty, as in the phrase no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: A cashier who surely has a job at a bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employed in' sets the word for doubt to work inside the word for bank. The surface shows a cashier, but the teller is simply one who tells, 'no doubt' is two separate pieces, and the bank is a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal synonym: one who tells people something is one who informs them or gives them notice.

clue.text: Male meets posh female philosopher

indicators.note: meets means comes up against, so the male word joins directly onto the piece that follows

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a male person or animal
gel is how upper-class English speech is caricatured as saying girl, as in jolly hockey-sticks gels

explanation.surface: A man is introduced to an upper-class woman who thinks deeply for a living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meets' joins HE to GEL, a caricature of how the English upper classes say girl. The definition is the German idealist thinker, not a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich of that name was a German idealist thinker, famed for his dialectic.

clue.text: Among men, a special ruler

parts.note: taken as written: the article is rearranged along with the other two words and lands at the front

indicators.note: special means out of the ordinary, so the words before it are taken out of their ordinary order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: One ruler stands out from other men as exceptional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'special' rearranges AMONG MEN A as one heap of letters, which is how the article, named last, comes to lead. The ruler is the king of Mycenae who led the Greeks against Troy in Homer's Iliad.
explanation.definitionFit: An example from Greek legend: the king of Mycenae who commanded the army that besieged Troy.

clue.text: Chicken about right? Put in oven

indicators.note: put in is an order to the solver: the oven word is to be placed inside the word for about

parts.note: re is the preposition meaning about or concerning, as at the head of a business letter
an oast is a kiln, an oven for drying hops, as in the oast houses of Kent in south-east England
R is the standard abbreviation for right, as in L and R

explanation.surface: The chicken looks more or less ready, so into the oven it goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in' is an instruction to the solver, not to a cook: the oven word goes inside the word for about. That oven is a hop-drying kiln, and the definition is 'Chicken' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind of it: a young bird of the right size to be cooked whole by dry heat.

clue.text: Inexperienced fellow talked of stock market activity

parts.note: green means new and untrained, as a green recruit is

indicators.note: talked of means spoken about, so the word for fellow is heard in speech and written with another spelling

parts.note: a fellow is a man, a male

explanation.surface: A novice chatted about trading in shares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'talked of' asks for MALE as spoken, which is then spelt MAIL. Greenmail is buying enough of a company's shares to threaten a takeover, so that the firm buys them back at a premium.
explanation.definitionFit: An example of it: buying a block of a company's shares to threaten a takeover, then selling them back at a premium.

clue.text: Very unpleasant lout, half-cut, finally staggers into party

indicators.note: half-cut says the word before it, lout, is cut in half and only its front half is kept
into sends the letter from staggers inside the word for party

parts.note: an at-home is a dated British term for a reception held in one's own house

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word right after it, staggers

explanation.surface: A nasty drunken yob eventually lurches into a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-cut', British slang for fairly drunk, keeps the front half of lout. 'finally' takes the last letter of staggers and 'into' puts it inside AT HOME, a dated name for a house party.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: something that arouses loathing is repulsive, thoroughly disagreeable.

clue.text: High up, overlooking house in Morecambe?

indicators.note: in places the two pieces before it inside the name that Morecambe suggests

parts.note: Eric Morecambe was half of Morecambe and Wise, Britain's best-loved comedy double act; the question mark flags him as one example of the name

indicators.note: in a down entry a piece that overlooks another stands above it, so up is written over the house

parts.note: ho is a standard abbreviation for house, seen on maps and in addresses

explanation.surface: Someone stands on high ground looking down on a house in the English seaside town of Morecambe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' stacks the first two pieces and 'in' puts them inside a first name. Morecambe is not the Lancashire seaside town but Eric Morecambe, of the British comedy duo Morecambe and Wise, who took his stage name from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym of mood: someone on a high is elated, intensely happy and excited.

clue.text: Gets stuck into poor-quality drink

parts.note: duff is British slang for useless or of poor quality, as in a duff battery
to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls

explanation.surface: Someone tucks eagerly into a cheap, nasty drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces sit side by side with no indicator. 'Gets stuck into' suggests tucking into a drink, but in British slang to get stuck into someone is to attack them, as is to duff them up.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms in British slang: both phrases mean attacking a person physically, giving them a beating.

clue.text: Fifty drowned in doomed German destroyer

indicators.note: something drowned lies under the surface, so the numeral is sunk within the letters that follow
doomed means fated to be wrecked, a loose way of saying the word after it is broken up and its letters put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Fifty sailors were lost when an ill-fated German warship went down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doomed' rearranges GERMAN into MANGER, and 'drowned in' sinks L inside it. The surface paints a warship going down with fifty sailors, but the destroyer is simply something that wrecks.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym by action: a person or machine that crushes and tears things ruins them, as the definition says.

clue.text: Confirm in writing, perhaps, banning extremists from meeting

indicators.note: the extremists of a word are the letters at its two extremes, and banning them strikes off its first and last letters

parts.note: things that are meeting are joining up, connecting; the word wanted is the -ing form of the verb to link

explanation.surface: A committee puts it on paper that hardliners are barred from its gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banning extremists from' strikes the first and last letters, L and G, off LINKING. To ink in an appointment is to make a pencilled entry in a diary definite, hence the 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: an arrangement first pencilled into a diary is made definite by going over it with a pen.

clue.text: Coat needed by sherpa in Tibet

indicators.note: needed by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A mountain guide working in Tibet cannot do without a warm jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needed by' signals that the answer lies inside 'sherpa in Tibet', running across the word breaks. The coat is not a garment but a layer brushed onto a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym as noun or verb: a layer of colour brushed onto a surface, or the act of applying one.

clue.text: Old professor's first university's work

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old, as in OT for Old Testament

indicators.note: first, coming after the possessive, asks for the opening letter of professor

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university, and this time the s after the apostrophe is kept as a letter

explanation.surface: A piece of research belongs to the first university where an elderly academic taught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes the opening letter of professor. The apostrophe-s on professor's is only grammar, but the one on university's is kept as the final letter after U.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym from Latin: the word for a labour or creation, used of a composer's numbered pieces.
